paras: The lynching of W. D. French took place in Greeley, Colorado, on the night of December 28-29, 1888, when a body of masked men broke into the county jail, took out French and hanged him to a tree. French, a cattle owner and farmer, was being held with three other men for the killing of Harry Woodbury at Evans about two weeks earlier. No member of the mob was identified, and most papers reported the lynching only as a short wire item.

According to the Omaha Bee, French and Woodbury had farmed together that season until a dispute over the division of 800 pounds of flour went to court and Woodbury won. French, his son, John Samples and John Hogan were then accused of breaking into Woodbury's house at Evans, four miles below Greeley, and shooting him dead in front of his wife and two children. An earlier Bee item gave a different version, saying French and six of his cowboys waylaid Woodbury, whom it called a laborer, on his way home from work. Sheriff Wollover and a posse captured the accused party at French's ranch, ten miles from Evans, and lodged them in the county jail at Greeley.

The Bee's Greeley correspondent reported that the masked men seized Sheriff Wollover and, failing to get the keys, tore away the brickwork around the jail door. They broke the locks, destroyed the cages, took French out and hanged him to a tree near the jail. The press-association dispatch said instead that the mob overpowered the jailer early in the morning and hanged French near the court house.

A coroner's inquest was in progress on December 29, but no clue to the lynchers had been found, and the wire reported that none of the mob were known. The coverage does not report the inquest's verdict or what became of French's son, Samples and Hogan, who remained in the jail.

Most papers carried the same brief dispatch, datelined Greeley or Denver, under headlines such as "Judge Lynch's Prey," "Lynched by a Greeley Mob" and "W. D. French Lynched for Murder." The dispatch stated as fact that French had "murdered Harry Woodbury," though he had not been tried. The Omaha Bee's longer telegram, headed "LYNCH LAW," called the Woodbury killing a "cowardly deed" by "villains" and described the lynchers as "indignant citizens" who could not wait for the law to take its course.

Eastern papers reduced the story to a single line in condensed-news columns on December 30 and 31. These briefs garbled details: the Portland Daily Press named the victim "A. D. French," and the Washington Evening Star placed the lynching at "Groesby" near Denver and called the murdered man "Henry Woodbury."

Accounts differ on the timing, with the Bee reporting the jailbreak "last night" in a December 29 telegram and the wire saying "early this morning," while one copy of the wire carried a December 28 dateline. The Bee placed the hanging near the jail and the wire near the court house, and the two Bee reports differ on how Woodbury was killed and by how many men.

bases: A body of masked men broke into the Greeley jail, took out a prisoner held for murder, and hanged him to a tree (A2, A3, A4).

French was hanged by 'a large body of masked men' or 'a mob' who broke him out of jail without any lawful authority (A2, A3); the Bee said they acted because they feared he might escape punishment for the killing of Harry Woodbury (A2).
The Omaha Bee's special telegram from Greeley (A2) and the separate press-association dispatch (A3, A4) agree on the jailbreak and hanging, and later briefs repeat it (A13, A14).

accounts.label: Omaha Bee special telegram from Greeley
accounts.gist: A large body of masked men seized the sheriff, broke through the jail's brickwork and cages, and hanged French near the jail; the inquest had found no clue, and the citizens apparently feared he might escape punishment.

accounts.label: Press-association wire (Greeley/Denver)
accounts.gist: A mob overpowered the jailer early in the morning, broke open the jail and hanged French to a tree near the court house; the men were unknown.

accounts.label: Evening Star brief
accounts.gist: French, a wealthy farmer near Denver, was taken from jail 'at Groesby' by a mob Friday night and hanged to the nearest tree for murdering his neighbor before the neighbor's family.

accounts.label: Omaha Bee, before the lynching
accounts.gist: French lost a lawsuit to Woodbury, then with six cowboys waylaid him on his way home from work and riddled him with bullets.

framing.detail: Headed 'LYNCH LAW. A Murderer Taken From the Greely, Colo., Jail and Hanged,' the Bee called the Woodbury killing 'shocking' and a 'cowardly deed' by 'villains' and explained the lynchers as 'indignant citizens' who could not wait for the law, without comment on the lynching itself.
The wire, under headlines such as 'Judge Lynch's Prey,' 'Lynched by a Greeley Mob' and 'W. D. French Lynched for Murder,' stated that French 'murdered' Woodbury as fact.
Eastern papers ran the story as a one-line item in condensed-news columns.
